q: Is Hatha yoga good for beginners?
What is the difference between Hatha and Vinyasa yoga?
What are the traditional Hatha yoga texts?
a: Hatha yoga is a broad, gentle foundational style that holds poses for longer periods with emphasis on alignment, breathing, and relaxation. It is excellent for beginners because of its slower pace and focus on basic asanas and proper alignment. In the West, Hatha is often used as a general term for any physical yoga practice, but traditional Hatha Yoga—as described in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika (15th century, attributed to Svatmarama)—includes shatkarmas (six cleansing practices), 15 primary asanas, pranayama, mudras, bandhas, and meditation aimed at purifying the body and preparing for Raja Yoga. Unlike Vinyasa's flowing breath-to-movement style, Hatha typically holds poses from 30 seconds to several minutes.

q: What is the sun salutation (Surya Namaskar)?
How is Vinyasa different from Ashtanga?
Is Vinyasa yoga good for beginners?
a: Vinyasa yoga emphasizes breath-synchronized movement, linking each inhale and exhale to a transition between poses, creating a continuous, dance-like flow. The Sun Salutation (Surya Namaskar) sequence is the foundation of most Vinyasa practices, typically including twelve poses per round: Mountain to Forward Fold, Half Lift, Plank, Chaturanga, Upward Dog, Downward Dog, and returning through the sequence. Unlike Ashtanga's fixed series and strict sequencing, Vinyasa classes vary widely in pace, difficulty, and sequence design—some are gentle and accessible for beginners, while others are fast-paced and physically demanding with music and heat-building sequences. The emphasis on smooth transitions (vinyasa krama) distinguishes it from Hatha's longer holds.

q: What are the Ashtanga series (Primary, Intermediate, Advanced)?
What is the Ashtanga vinyasa count?
a: Ashtanga yoga, as taught by K. Pattabhi Jois, follows a fixed sequence of poses organized into six series. The Primary Series (Yoga Chikitsa) focuses on forward folds, hip opening, and detoxification; the Intermediate Series (Nadi Shodhana) emphasizes backbends and energetic cleansing; and the Advanced Series (Sthira Bhaga—four levels) develops strength, grace, and devotion. Practice is traditionally done six days a week (excluding Saturdays and moon days) either in Led Class (teacher counts the vinyasa in Sanskrit) or Mysore style (students practice their series at their own pace with individual teacher guidance). The Tristhana method integrates three focal points: asana (posture), vinyasa (breath-synchronized movement), and drishti (gazing point). Each pose has a specific vinyasa count (number of movements to enter and exit).

q: What props are used in Iyengar yoga?
How does Iyengar yoga use alignment?
a: Iyengar yoga is characterized by meticulous alignment, extended pose holds, and the use of props (belts, blocks, blankets, wall ropes, chairs, bolsters, and sandbags) to make poses accessible to all bodies and to refine the expression of each asana. B.K.S. Iyengar, author of the seminal text 'Light on Yoga,' developed this method emphasizing standing poses as foundational, inversions for health and longevity, and restorative practices for healing. Sequencing progresses systematically from simple to complex poses, and poses are held for relatively long durations (30 seconds to several minutes) to develop strength, stability, and body awareness. Therapeutic applications include sequences for specific conditions such as back pain, hypertension, scoliosis, and women's health (menstruation, pregnancy, menopause).

q: What is hot yoga versus Bikram yoga?
What is the Bikram room temperature?
a: Bikram yoga consists of a fixed sequence of 26 postures (including two breathing exercises) practiced in a room heated to 105°F (40.6°C) with 40% humidity for exactly 90 minutes. Founded by Bikram Choudhury, this style follows a strict dialogue (the teacher recites the same instructions for each class). Unlike general 'hot yoga' (which encompasses many styles practiced in heated rooms), true Bikram yoga adheres to a trademarked sequence and studio franchise system. Bikram Choudhury faced multiple sexual assault allegations and was ordered to pay $6.5 million in a 2016 lawsuit, leading to bankruptcy and the decline of the Bikram franchise. Contemporary hot yoga classes often borrow elements of Bikram's sequence and heat but under different names and liberated from the trademarked format.

q: What is a kriya in Kundalini yoga?
What is the White Tantric Yoga?
a: Kundalini yoga, as taught by Yogi Bhajan (3HO organization), is a dynamic practice combining kriyas (specific sequences of postures, breath, movement, sound, and meditation), pranayama (especially Breath of Fire—rapid diaphragmatic breathing), mantra chanting (from Sikh tradition), mudras, and intense concentration. The stated goal is to awaken the dormant energy (kundalini) at the base of the spine and raise it through the chakras to the crown chakra for spiritual enlightenment. Uniquely, practitioners often wear white clothing and turbans (to expand the aura and contain energy). A typical class includes tuning in with the mantra 'Ong Namo Guru Dev Namo,' a warm-up, a central kriya, relaxation (often with a gong), meditation, and closing with a song and blessing.

q: What is the difference between yin and restorative yoga?
What props are used in restorative yoga?
How long do you hold yin yoga poses?
Is yin yoga good for stress?
a: Restorative yoga uses extensive props (bolsters, blankets, blocks, sandbags) to support the body in passive poses held for 5-20 minutes, allowing deep relaxation and activating the parasympathetic nervous system. The goal is complete surrender and ease—no muscular effort is required. Yin yoga, while similar in its long holds, targets the deeper connective tissues (fascia, ligaments, tendons, joints) through moderate stress (sensation, not pain) applied for 3-5 minutes per pose. Yin draws on Taoist and Chinese medicine concepts, working with the meridian energy lines and targeting the yin (stable, dense) tissues of the body. Both styles are excellent for stress reduction, but yin is more actively challenging on the connective tissue level, while restorative is purely supportive relaxation and healing (often recommended for trauma-sensitive or injury recovery contexts).

q: What are the main yin yoga poses?
What is the dragon pose in yin?
What is the shoe lace pose in yin?
What is a yin yoga sequence?
a: Yin yoga poses are adapted from traditional asanas to target connective tissues with long, passive holds. Key yin poses include: Dragon (a deep lunge targeting hip flexors and psoas), Shoelace (external rotation of the hips), Caterpillar (forward fold for the spine and hamstrings), Saddle (intense quad and hip flexor stretch), Swan/Pigeon (deep external hip rotation and gluteal release), Snail (shoulder and spinal compression), Seal (gentle backbend), Butterfly (groin and inner thigh stretch), Frog (hip adductor stretch), and Happy Baby (lower back and sacrum). Teachers often combine poses in thematic sequences based on meridian theory from Chinese medicine (e.g., a Liver/Gallbladder meridian sequence targets the sides of the body and inner legs). Paul Grilley and Sarah Powers are key teachers who codified modern yin yoga, linking it to Taoist and anatomical principles.
